title: Erasmus Latin through Naibbe v2
method: Michael A. Greshko, The Naibbe cipher (2025), https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2025.2566408; implementation https://github.com/greshko/naibbe-cipher/tree/5145f526b52741a6dca14201147f687e62c7162e. Use the published Naibbe v2 tables and 78-card weights, RESPACING=17 and UNAMBIGUOUS=True. Apply clean_line to the joined pinned la_erasmus reference blocks and take up to the first 32,000 cleaned letters (28,969 available; SHA-256 ff6426801002dc2fe83b46f3d91a385334174296a9dc0c2d7c5bea2d3d78a71b), dropping original word breaks. Seed Python random with 20261128 and encrypt in one continuous call; each ciphertext token represents one or two source letters, with randomized table choices and without original word breaks. Before optional space removal, arrange consecutive tokens into lines of eight; the last line can be shorter. No position or target-fact rules are applied. Practice split advisory: 5/28 facts, F-013, F-014, F-017, F-024 and F-031; all others missed. This differs in plaintext, token-space handling and layout from the Italian R-049, so it is not a controlled language comparison.
